storm.summary_layperson: No storms in the area or heading toward the cove tonight — mostly sunny skies with essentially zero instability, so the 5–10 PM window should stay dry.
storm.local_effect_blurb: No storms are around to blunt tonight, so the marine layer isn't being tested — for reference the air–water gap is running 7–8°F this evening and narrowing slightly as the air cools.
storm.detail_html:
No storms are on the board tonight. KOKX radar shows no echoes approaching the cove, current instability is essentially zero (CAPE 0 J/kg per the 19Z HRRR cycle), and there are no active NWS watches, warnings, or advisories for the area.

The Area Forecast Discussion does flag thunderstorm chances, but not for this window — the mentions are for Thursday afternoon/evening (a slow-moving cold front) and again Sunday. Tonight's 5 PM–10 PM window sits in a quiet gap between those two systems.

The backdoor cold-front check (Boston/Providence/Groton sentinels) is clear: KBOS and KPVD are both west-southwesterly and KGON is south — none have flipped northeast. August 19 is also just outside the core backdoor season, so this risk is negligible regardless.

Because there's no storm to modify, the marine layer's usual storm-blunting role isn't in play tonight. For reference: the air–water gap (a proxy for how much buffer the Sound would offer) is running about 7–8°F through the early evening and is projected to narrow toward 6°F by 6 PM as the air cools faster than the water holds its temperature. The forecast only extends that trend to 6 PM this cycle, so the overnight numbers aren't available — academic tonight since nothing is inbound.

wind.tactics_blurb: Sea breeze holding W/WNW at 5–7 kt through 6 PM — an atypical axis for the cove, channeled down the Sound from the NYC/Westchester direction, with steadier pressure mid-course than tight to the CT shore. It fades after 6 PM and should be dead by 8 PM, about 30–45 minutes after the 7:46 PM sunset — don't plan on breeze for a late race.
wind.tactics_detail_html:
Today classifies as a pure thermal sea-breeze day, though an atypical one for this stretch of the CT shore. The land–water temperature gap (deltaT) is 7.9°F — above the 5°F threshold that gets a sea breeze going, but just under the 8°F gate the pipeline uses to fully trust a mature direction. The background gradient wind is light and offshore (Westchester's KHPN reading W at 7 kt), which is exactly the calm-to-offshore, under-8-kt signature of a pure thermal day rather than a gradient-reinforced one.

What's unusual is the axis: only 40% of CT-coast stations are reading southerly, and RYC itself is sitting at WNW 294° rather than the classic S–SSW sea-breeze direction for this coastline. HRRR agrees the flow is out of the W/WNW quadrant but is running about 17° behind the observed veer — a divergence large enough that station obs are being trusted over the raw model for the next couple of hours. Practically, this reads as a west-end-of-the-Sound sea breeze setting up channeled down the Sound from the NYC/Westchester direction rather than the pure south flow the cove usually sees.

Because W–WNW is a channeled direction rather than a straight shot up the cove, expect it to hold fairly steady in direction but with holes close to the CT shore and better, steadier pressure mid-course. Favor the middle of the course rather than committing hard to either shore.

Shift character through 6 PM should be the normal oscillating pattern of a mature afternoon sea breeze (it's already past the morning ramping window) — play the shifts, don't commit hard either way. After 6 PM the thermal starts fading on schedule and collapses within about 30–45 minutes of the 7:46 PM sunset, since there's no onshore gradient tailwind to keep it going once the sun goes down. By 8 PM expect light and variable, essentially unraceable air.

Data note: HRRR's hourly wind grids only came through for 5 PM and 6 PM this cycle (later forecast hours failed to fetch/parse) — the 7 PM–10 PM figures above are extrapolated from the sea-breeze collapse framework rather than pulled directly from the model, so treat them as directional guidance, not a precise forecast.
